prompts.prompt2:
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the Umbraco MCP server.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP server won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP server.

Always use the MCP server to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

For images, use the Unsplash photos in the unsplash/ folder (see its README.md) and import them into the media library. Don't download other images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.

finalReport:
The blog is built and running. The front page and both posts return HTTP 200, with no "Could not render component" fallbacks and the images and CSS loading. I only fetched the pages and never opened them in a browser, so I haven't seen the Tailwind styling.

**To view it:** the site is running now from `dotnet run` in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco`. Open `http://localhost:41576/` or `https://localhost:44317/`. The backoffice login is admin@example.com / 1234567890.

**What I built**
- **Content modeling:**
  - **Block elements:** `heroBlock`, `blogPostListBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock` and `quoteBlock`.
  - **Composition:** `seoComposition`, with a meta title and description.
  - **Pages:** `blogHome`, allowed under `siteRoot`, and `blogPost`, each with a block grid property.
  - **Block grid data types:** "Blog Home Block Grid" and "Blog Post Block Grid".
  - **Where they live:** I filed everything in the matching document type folders. Umbraco filed the data types under `/Custom/`.
- **Content:** I created the "MCP Blog" front page under WWW and gave it the domain `/`. It has a hero block and a post-list block. Under it are two published posts:
  - "MCP turns your AI from a talker into a doer"
  - "One protocol, endless integrations"
- **Media:** I imported five Unsplash photos into a "Blog" media folder. The posts' captions credit the photographers of the inline images.
- **Razor and frontend:**
  - **Block rendering:** pages call `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`. Each block has a `blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml` adapter that maps to a plain model and invokes a ViewComponent. There are no custom renderers or wrapper models.
  - **Files:** the plain models are in `Models/Blocks/` and the ViewComponents in `ViewComponents/`. The component views, `_Layout` and the two page templates are all new.
  - **Styling:** Tailwind styling is in `site.css`, built with `npm install` and `npm run build` in the Frontend project.
- **Everything through MCP:** the document types, data types, templates, media and content were all created through the MCP server, in the order you specified. I wrote no migrations.

**Not verified or worth knowing**
- I haven't seen the page in a browser, so the layout and styling are untested visually.
- `UmbracoContext` is nullable in the list adapter, so I read it with `?.`.
- I changed `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml` to import the project's models namespaces.
- I didn't check that uSync exported the schema to `uSync/`.
- The `blogHome` and `blogPost` types show "allowed in library" as true, which I didn't set deliberately. It's harmless for this demo.
- There is no git repository here, so nothing is committed.
